P380
Treatment resistant jerky stiff person syndrome
T. P. Harrower, R. Barker, J. Baron, A. Coles (Cambridge, United
Kingdom)
Background: Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is a well recognized autoim-
mune mediated condition with an association with antibodies to glutamic
acid decarboxylase (GAD). Less well deﬁned is the condition of Jerky SPS,
an atypical form of SPS.
Methods: Here we present a case of a 28 male who initially presented
with neck and back pain, and generalised stiffness associated with jerks in
his neck. Over the next few months the jerky muscle activity spread to
involve his shoulder girdle (see video). Clinical examination conﬁrmed the
presence of regular spasms resembling myoclonic jerks in the shoulder
girdle region with generalised stiffness but no other general or neurological
deﬁcits.
Results: Besides the presence of an elevated anti-GAD titre initially 12
rising to 105 (normal range less than 10 ng/ml) tests have been normal
including neuroimaging, somatosensory evoked responses. But electro-
myography demonstrated episodes of spontaneous motor activity. General
investigations (including tumour markers, whole body CT and FDG-PET
scanning) have failed to demonstrate an occult malignancy. Immunomodu-
latory therapy including, steroids, plasma exchange, intravenous immuno-
globulin and rituximab (monoclonal antibody directed against B cells) has
reduced the anti-GAD antibody titre to within normal limits (3.6 ng/ml) but
has failed to produce any clinical beneﬁt beyond a mild response to high
doses of benzodiazepines during 36 months of follow-up.
Conclusions: We therefore demonstrate a case of Jerky SPS reafﬁrming
the presence of an atypical SPS phenotype in the absence of a malignancy
which has failed to clinically respond to immunotherapy despite a sero-
logical response.
